item.title: Americans Are Feeling the Cost of Travel, But Still Making Room for It
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Americans are increasingly feeling the financial strain of travel, but new research from Longwoods International suggests that rising costs have not displaced vacations from the priority list. In a September 2026 tracking study, 75 percent of travelers said they believe travel is becoming too expensive, up from 64 percent a year earlier. Yet 81 percent said vacations are among the things they most look forward to each year, while 55 percent said they are willing to reduce spending in other areas to fund their trips.

The study also points to the emotional value travelers place on time away. Seventy-four percent said the experiences gained through travel are more important to them than acquiring additional material belongings, while 84 percent said traveling with friends and family brings them closer together, up from 78 percent a year ago. At the same time, near-term travel planning has softened somewhat, with 87 percent reporting trips planned within the next six months compared with 93 percent last October. The survey was conducted September 1–4 among 1,000 U.S. adults, with demographic quotas designed to reflect the U.S. population.

The Curated Take: The numbers suggest that the travel conversation is shifting from whether Americans want to travel to what they are willing to give up to keep traveling. Rising costs may be forcing more deliberate choices, but the willingness to redirect spending toward experiences indicates that travel remains tied to something deeper than discretionary consumption. For the industry, that could mean greater emphasis on the emotional and relational value of a trip, particularly when travelers are making harder decisions about where their money goes.

item.title: Southern Ocean Lodge Joins MICHELIN’s Highest-Rated Wilderness Hotels
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Southern Ocean Lodge on Kangaroo Island has been elevated to Three MICHELIN Keys, the guide’s highest hotel distinction, as eight properties across the Beckons luxury lodge portfolio receive recognition in the 2026 MICHELIN Key Hotels selection. Perched on the cliffs of South Australia’s Kangaroo Island, Southern Ocean Lodge was recognized for its modern architecture, remote setting and access to wildlife and nature experiences. It is one of only 18 hotels worldwide to receive its first Three Keys in 2026, placing it among a particularly small group of properties recognized for an extraordinary stay.

The broader Beckons portfolio demonstrates how MICHELIN’s hotel recognition is increasingly reaching properties where the surrounding landscape is central to the experience. Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge in Canada and Tierra Patagonia in Chile retained Three Keys, while Longitude 131°, Capella Lodge, Silky Oaks Lodge, Huka Lodge and Tierra Atacama received Two Keys. Across destinations ranging from the Australian outback and tropical rainforest to the Andes and New Zealand’s Waikato River, the properties share an emphasis on small-scale hospitality, local knowledge and experiences shaped by their environments.

The Curated Take: The most revealing part of the Beckons recognition is its geographic consistency. These aren’t interchangeable luxury lodges with a shared design template. Their settings dictate what the experience becomes, whether that means wildlife on Kangaroo Island, the desert around Uluṟu or the wilderness of Torres del Paine. Southern Ocean Lodge’s move to Three Keys underscores a broader shift in luxury travel toward properties where architecture, hospitality and access to the natural world are inseparable from the destination itself.

item.title: Barcelona’s Food Scene Becomes a Guided Experience Through Time Out’s Lens
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Devour Tours and Time Out have joined forces for a new food experience in Barcelona that turns Time Out’s restaurant recommendations into a guided culinary journey. Time Out Market Barcelona: Tapas Tour & Market Visit is limited to 10 guests and moves through the Gothic Quarter before arriving at Time Out Market Barcelona. Along the way, travelers visit a bookshop-turned-wine-bar, an 80-year-old bodega and a tapas bar that has remained largely unchanged since 1945, sampling Spanish specialties and local drinks along the route.

The three-hour experience is designed around the practical knowledge that can make navigating a city’s food culture more rewarding, with guides explaining what to order, how to approach each stop and where local traditions fit into the meal. The final stop at Time Out Market Barcelona brings the experience toward the waterfront, with views of the port and additional tastes including paella and churros with chocolate. Rather than presenting Barcelona’s food scene as a checklist of recommended restaurants, the collaboration turns editorial discovery into a route travelers can experience firsthand.

The Curated Take: There is a useful distinction between knowing where to eat in a city and understanding how to eat there. This collaboration plays in that space, combining Time Out’s editorial perspective with Devour’s local guides and access. For travelers, the value is less about visiting a series of famous food stops than gaining context around the rituals, neighborhoods and long-standing establishments that give Barcelona its culinary identity.

item.title: Zannier Hotels Brings Conservation to a New Mediterranean Setting
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
With the opening of Zannier Île de Bendor in the South of France, Zannier Hotels is extending its conservation-first approach into the Mediterranean. Set on a private, car-free island off Bandol, the project centers on renaturation, with more than 15 percent additional trees, 1,500 square metres of de-paved land and landscaping composed of 70 percent Mediterranean plant species. The restoration also brought 25 existing buildings up to modern environmental standards and reused 25,000 tons of excavated material on the island, illustrating an approach that works with an existing landscape rather than simply building over it.

The Mediterranean project joins a portfolio in which conservation strategies are tailored to each destination. At Zannier Bãi San Hô in Vietnam, coral restoration and marine cleanup support the surrounding ecosystem, while in Namibia, Zannier Omaanda’s reserve works to protect threatened wildlife and Zannier Sonop operates with solar power, a self-sustained water system and extensive waste recycling. Across the portfolio, the focus extends beyond reducing a hotel’s footprint to restoring ecosystems, conserving water and soil, eliminating waste and working with local environments and communities.

The Curated Take: The more interesting sustainability story in luxury hospitality is increasingly what happens to a place, not simply what happens inside a hotel. Zannier’s model acknowledges that conservation cannot look the same in a Mediterranean island, a Vietnamese coastline or a Namibian wildlife reserve. Île de Bendor is particularly compelling because its environmental strategy is built around restoring an already developed landscape, suggesting that luxury and regeneration can coexist without requiring a destination to be untouched in the first place.

item.title: Karma Spa Blends Japanese and Indonesian Traditions in a New Bali Wellness Ritual
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Karma Spa at Karma Kandara in Ungasan, Bali, has introduced the Aroma Escape Japanese Head Spa Treatment, combining Japanese bathing traditions with the botanical approach of traditional Indonesian cream baths. Set on the resort’s clifftops overlooking the Indian Ocean, the ritual begins with deep scalp cleansing before moving into massage techniques focused on acupressure points across the head, neck and shoulders. Nourishing hair treatments are incorporated throughout, with the experience designed to promote circulation, relaxation and a greater sense of mental clarity.

The treatment reflects Karma Spa’s broader approach to destination wellness, which combines local healing practices with contemporary therapies. Its therapist team is trained in anatomy and includes practitioners certified in Reiki and local healing arts, while the spa’s offerings range from traditional Balinese rituals to more contemporary experiences such as an ocean-view magnesium ice bath. The Aroma Escape adds another layer by bringing together two distinct cultural approaches to bathing and body care within Bali’s dramatic coastal setting.

The Curated Take: The most compelling aspect of the Aroma Escape is its cultural conversation. Rather than presenting Japanese head spa therapy as a trend transplanted into Bali, the treatment places it alongside an established Indonesian wellness tradition. That combination makes the experience feel more connected to the destination and reflects a broader evolution in luxury wellness toward rituals with cultural context, rather than treatments designed simply to relax.

item.title: Nashville by the Book
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Nashville is a city of distinct rhythms. Beyond the neon of Lower Broadway and the steady pulse of studio sessions, there is a quieter, more grounded tempo waiting in the residential neighborhoods and historic squares of Middle Tennessee. For travelers looking to unclench from screen-heavy routines, the region’s independent bookstores offer an immediate sense of place—a chance to step off the itinerary, run a hand across textured paper, and listen to the city at human scale.

The Greater Nashville Haven

In East Nashville, The Bookshop feels less like a store and more like a sunlit breathing space. Owned by former book editor Joelle Herr, every title in the small, minimalist room is displayed with intentional visual clarity. Clean wood lines, natural light, and a hyper-edited selection of fiction, design, and art invite you to move slowly, turning a 10-minute drop-in into an hour of quiet discovery.

Across the Cumberland River in Green Hills, Parnassus Books serves as Nashville’s undisputed literary anchor. Co-owned by novelist Ann Patchett and bookseller Karen Hayes, Parnassus has the warm authority of a neighborhood institution. Hardcovers sit on long display tables, staff members share unhurried recommendations, and the shop’s rescue dogs roam the aisles with gentle purpose. It is a space built on deep community connections, where signed first editions sit beside local histories and new voices.

Driving south into Williamson County, the pace shifts from neighborhood streets to historic brick corridors. In downtown Franklin, Landmark Booksellers occupies an 1808 commercial building that has weathered two centuries of Southern history. Inside, the floorboards creak underfoot, and the air carries the rich, dry scent of vintage paper. With more than 60,000 volumes—from rare leather-bound classics to signed first editions—owners Joel and Carol Tomlin welcome visitors with the warmth of old friends, making it easy to lose an entire afternoon in the stacks.

As dusk falls between Franklin and Nashville, The Raven Book Lounge in Brentwood reimagines the bookstore for the evening hours. Low lamps, overstuffed velvet armchairs, and a craft cocktail bar create a moody, comfortable setting where a quiet drink and a new chapter seamlessly coexist.

Further on the region’s periphery, small-town stops offer their own quiet charm. In Greenbrier, The Storybook Cottage combines tea, house-made drinks, and cozy reading nooks with an intimate community theater space. To the southeast in historic downtown Murfreesboro, The Grand Exchange Bookstore pairs new and used titles with house plants, local art, and neighborhood book club gatherings.

Where to Stay in Nashville

1 Hotel Nashville: An eco-conscious sanctuary in the city center featuring biophilic design, reclaimed wood accents, Ivy-draped exterior walls, and a restorative spa atmosphere.

The Hermitage Hotel: Nashville’s iconic downtown landmark, offering 1910 Beaux-Arts architecture, spacious suites, and refined dining at Drusie & Darr by Jean-Georges.

Southall Farm & Inn (Franklin): A 325-acre countryside retreat of rolling hills, working orchards, and agrarian wellness, located just minutes from downtown Franklin’s historic square.

Worth the Day Trip: Four Regional Standouts

If your schedule allows you to expand beyond Middle Tennessee, four curated destinations capture the distinct literary character of the state’s outer regions.

Chattanooga — The Reading Room: Merging used book culture with industrial design, floor-to-ceiling shelves line exposed brick walls under vintage chandeliers, paired with a full craft cocktail bar that donates a portion of sales to the local public library foundation.

Knoxville — Addison’s: Tucked into downtown Knoxville, this quiet sanctuary specializes in rare, antiquarian, and out-of-print volumes, making it an essential stop for collectors seeking leather-bound history.

The Smokies — The Next Chapter Bookshop (Gatlinburg): Nestled in Gatlinburg’s historic Arts & Crafts Community, this mountain haven curates regional writing and Appalachian stories perfect for settling into a cabin retreat.

Memphis — Burke’s Bookstore: Operating in the historic Cooper-Young neighborhood since 1875, one of the nation’s oldest indie booksellers offers generations of literary heritage along the Mississippi River bluffs.

item.title: W Bali Brings Fashion and Padel Together With Club Lacoste
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
W Bali – Seminyak is bringing fashion and sport together with the arrival of Club Lacoste, marking the French brand’s longest-running Club Lacoste partnership in Asia Pacific. The collaboration introduces two padel courts alongside an official Lacoste boutique, creating a dedicated space where the fast-growing racket sport meets the brand’s fashion and lifestyle identity. The partnership also marks Lacoste’s first dedicated padel capsule, including rackets and footwear, alongside apparel, eyewear, watches, fragrances and accessories.

Open to both resort guests and the wider community, Club Lacoste positions padel as a social experience as much as a sport. Players can move between the courts and retail space, while W Bali’s broader setting adds dining, beachfront atmosphere and opportunities for gathering to the experience. With padel’s popularity continuing to expand internationally, the collaboration reflects how hotels are increasingly incorporating the sport into their lifestyle offerings rather than treating courts as a standalone amenity.

The Curated Take: Club Lacoste is an interesting example of where luxury hospitality and contemporary sport are converging. Padel’s appeal is partly its accessibility and social character, making it particularly well suited to a resort environment where the experience can continue after the match. In Bali, Lacoste gets more than a court and a retail space. It gets a setting that naturally connects sport, fashion, leisure and community.

item.title: IHG Hotels & Resorts Joins the Journey to Rugby World Cup 2027
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
IHG Hotels & Resorts has been named Official Hotel Partner of Men’s Rugby World Cup 2027, connecting its global hotel network with what will be the largest edition of the tournament to date. Taking place across Australia from October 1 to November 13, 2027, the tournament will bring 24 teams and 52 matches to seven Host Cities, creating a significant travel occasion for fans arriving from around the world. IHG will welcome teams, officials and supporters while using its hotel portfolio and IHG One Rewards platform to connect travelers with the tournament experience.

The partnership also extends a relationship between IHG and the sport that spans more than two decades, including partnerships with Rugby Australia, SANZAAR, Six Nations Rugby and the British & Irish Lions. For travelers following the tournament across Australia, the hotel becomes part of the journey between matches and cities, with hospitality offering a natural meeting point for fans before and after games. The scale of the 2027 tournament also gives travelers an opportunity to experience Australia beyond the stadiums, from its host cities to the destinations connected by the tournament route.

The Curated Take: Major sporting events increasingly function as travel stories in their own right, giving fans a reason to explore a country rather than simply attend a match. Rugby World Cup 2027 has the potential to turn Australia’s seven Host Cities into chapters of a larger journey, and IHG’s role puts hotels directly into that travel narrative. For travelers, the appeal is not only where they watch the rugby, but what they discover between matches.

item.title: Four Seasons Singapore Puts Intimate Dining at the Center of the Wedding
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For couples choosing a wedding built around a smaller circle of family and friends, Four Seasons Hotel Singapore is placing intimate dining and distinctive settings at the heart of the celebration. On the hotel’s 20th floor, Windows East and Windows West offer private venues with floor-to-ceiling windows, outdoor patios and panoramic views across Singapore, creating an elevated setting for ceremonies, cocktails and dinners of up to 100 guests.

The experience extends beyond the venue itself, with individually plated six- and seven-course menus from MICHELIN-Selected Jiang-Nan Chun and opportunities to gather at Nobu Bar for welcome cocktails, pre-wedding celebrations or late-night toasts. Couples can also make one of the hotel’s restaurants the setting itself, with exclusive buyouts available at Nobu, Jiang-Nan Chun and One-Ninety. The result is a wedding experience shaped as much by food and atmosphere as by the ceremony, with each restaurant offering a distinctly different culinary and social character.

The Curated Take: Intimate weddings are increasingly less about scaling down a traditional celebration and more about designing something deliberately personal. Four Seasons Singapore’s approach plays into that shift by treating dining as part of the occasion’s identity rather than simply another element of the reception. For couples who would rather spend an evening around one beautifully considered table than host a large ballroom affair, the combination of Singapore views, restaurant-level cuisine and private spaces offers a more intimate way to celebrate without sacrificing a sense of occasion.

item.title: Conrad Koh Samui Creates a Private World Above the Gulf of Thailand
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Conrad Koh Samui is preparing to unveil The Pearl, a 766-square-metre Presidential Villa positioned at the resort’s highest point overlooking the Gulf of Thailand and the Five Islands. More than an expansive accommodation, the two-level retreat is designed as a private world where dining, entertainment, wellness and relaxation can unfold without leaving the villa. An upper entertaining level includes a sweeping terrace, private bar, living room and catering kitchen, while the lower level centers on a master suite and dedicated wellness sanctuary.

The Pearl’s private wellness facilities include a couple’s treatment room, sauna, steam room, hot and cold hydrotherapy plunges and a fitness space, extending the growing luxury travel emphasis on personalized wellness into the guest’s own accommodation. Outside, a 20-metre infinity pool, private cinema and sunken dining pavilion reinforce the villa’s residential character. Natural stone, warm woods and details inspired by Thai timber construction connect the contemporary design to Koh Samui’s landscape and architectural traditions, while views of the Five Islands provide a constant sense of place.

The Curated Take: The Pearl reflects a broader shift in high-end hospitality from simply offering a larger villa to creating an entirely self-contained experience. Here, privacy is not just about seclusion. Guests can move from movement and hydrotherapy to a chef-led dinner, sunset drinks or a film under the stars without ever leaving their own private environment. It is a distinctly contemporary interpretation of the resort escape, where the destination remains visible and present, even when the guest chooses not to venture beyond the villa.
